cards.text: This one's a Maskil of David, from after Doeg the Edomite, one of Saul's servants (1 Samuel 21:7), went to King Saul and told him, “David has gone to the house of Ahimelech.” Ahimelech was a priest (1 Samuel 21:1). David opens this psalm with a question for a mighty man, and friend, it is NOT a compliment.

cards.question: David asks the mighty man why he's bragging. What does David say the mighty man boasts of?

cards.text: Then, right next to all that bragging, David drops one quiet line about God. No hype. It just sits there and outlasts everything around it.

cards.question: Right after his question to the mighty man, David says the ___ of God endures all day long.

cards.text: Then David zooms in on the man's mouth. He calls him a worker of deceit, and his tongue devises destruction. That tongue needs a WARNING LABEL.

cards.question: David says the mighty man's tongue devises destruction. What does David compare that tongue to?
David says the mighty man loves speaking truth more than falsehood.

cards.text: Then comes a Selah. Breathe. And then David goes RIGHT back at that tongue, because he is not finished with it.

cards.question: David calls the mighty man a deceitful tongue. What kind of words does David say that tongue loves?

cards.text: Now the psalm turns from what the mighty man does to what God will do. And all that bragging is about to hit a wall.

cards.question: What does David say God will surely do to the mighty man?

answers.text: Bring him down to everlasting ruin
Give him a long and quiet life
Make him a ruler over Israel

cards.question: David says God will snatch the mighty man up and tear him away from his tent.

cards.text: And God will uproot him from the land of the living. Selah, and then David pictures the righteous watching it all happen.

cards.question: When God brings the mighty man down, the righteous will see and ___. They will ___ the evildoer.

cards.text: The righteous point at the fallen man and say exactly where it went wrong: he leaned on the wrong thing. Friend, I spent years in a drawer leaning on dead batteries that SWORE they still had a charge, so I am in no position to judge.

cards.question: The righteous say the man didn't make God his refuge. What did he trust instead?
The righteous say the fallen man strengthened himself by helping others.

cards.text: Then David turns it around with two little words, and now he's talking about himself. The mighty man got uprooted, but David pictures himself as something growing right where it belongs.

cards.question: David says he is like a flourishing ___ tree in the house of God.
Unlike the man who trusted his wealth, David says he trusts in the loving devotion of God forever and ever.

cards.text: And David closes with a promise to praise God forever. No end date. No snooze button. FOREVER.

cards.question: Why does David say he will praise God forever?
David says he will wait on God's name, because it is good. Where will he wait?

answers.text: In the presence of God's saints
In the court of King Saul

findings.problem: The right answer "Evil" is one word, while the wrong answers are two and three words ("His victories", "His family name"), so the right answer stands out by its shape.

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.

findings.problem: The card asks the baker to guess which image the poem uses for the tongue (razor, fire or arrow). Nothing on the earlier cards points to a razor, so this is the same kind of detail guess as the bad Psalm 23 example (oil, myrrh or perfume).

rule.text: Never ask the baker to guess the next words of a line.

findings.problem: Psalm 52:3 opens with "You love evil more than good." No card tells or asks this line. Card 7 covers only falsehood and truth, and card 8 skips straight to the Selah.

rule.text: When the baker leaves Prep, they understand the whole passage without missing an important detail.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The card asks the baker to guess the poem's wording: words that devour, flatter or curse. Card 8 gives no context that would let the baker reason toward "devours" over "flatters", which also fits a deceitful tongue.

rule.text: Never ask the baker to guess the next words of a line.

findings.problem: The setup line "all that bragging is about to hit a wall" rules out both wrong answers on card 2 ("Give him a long and quiet life", "Make him a ruler over Israel"). The answer is given away before the question is asked.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: Both wrong answers are rewards ("Give him a long and quiet life", "Make him a ruler over Israel") for a man the psalm has just condemned as evil and deceitful. That makes them close to silly, and the right answer is obvious.

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.

findings.problem: The baker has to guess two words of the line, "fear" and "mock", against "cheer", "pity" and "forget". Card 4 says only that the righteous are watching. Nothing lets the baker reason toward fear and then mocking, and "cheer" fits the setup just as well.

rule.text: Never ask the baker to guess the next words of a line.

findings.problem: The card asks the baker to guess what kind of tree (olive, cedar or fig). This is a pure detail guess about the poem's wording, the same as the bad Psalm 23 example. Card 9 gives nothing that points to an olive tree.

rule.text: Never ask the baker to guess the next words of a line.

findings.problem: This story card has four sentences: "And David closes with a promise to praise God forever." / "No end date." / "No snooze button." / "FOREVER."

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: Most story cards read as mildly pleasant rather than laugh-out-loud funny. Examples are stop 1 card 1 ("it is NOT a compliment"), stop 1 card 3, stop 1 card 8 and stop 2 card 1. Only stop 2 card 6 (the dead batteries) reaches for a real laugh.

rule.text: If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.
